verdict.reasoning: Patient says: "my chest has been feeling really tight" and when asked how long: "for about... three hours now."

Patient: "Yeah, like a little bit, um. Yeah, a little bit short of breath, not too bad" and later: "It does when I'm walking up stairs, I do feel like, I have a little bit, more short of breath than I would normally be" and "I'm definitely not short of breath at rest."
Patient: "I'm feeling a bit wheezy, as well. Kind of cough , coughing"; Doctor: "And are you coughing up anything?" Patient: "Uh, no." supporting a wheeze and non-productive (slight) cough.
Patient: "You know I had a cold last week... I had a sore throat, I had a runny nose..." and later: "the runny nose isn't as bad any more."
Patient: "Yeah, but the cough's kind of stuck around" and when asked if worse at night: "it gets a little bit worse at night but, basically, just pretty consistent."
Doctor: "you wouldn't say you've got chest pains? It's more of a tight chest, is it?" Patient: "No, not really pain, it's more like, tight."
Patient: "I'm definitely not short of breath at rest" and "when I'm walking up stairs, I do feel like, I have a little bit, more short of breath than I would normally be."

Patient: "Yeah, yeah, I have asthma"; "then I have like, a hayfever"; "my mum has eczema, and my dad has asthma, ohh, when I was young, I also had eczema"; "And I had a milk protein allergy, when I was young too."

Patient: "when I was in high school, I had to have a tube put down my throat" and confirms staying in hospital for a few days; later: "I think I was like seventeen. Sixteen maybe." indicating severe exacerbation around age 16–17 requiring intubation and hospitalization.
Patient: "you know the um, uh, Ventolin. It's called uh, Salbutamol. I got that one" and Doctor plans use "with Ventolin as a PRN ... when you need to" indicating as-needed use.

Patient: "then I have a steroid, a Clenil, Clenil inhaler"; "I forgot to bring it with me, so I haven't really in the past week"; "because ... they ran out" and Doctor: "you've, you haven't got any Clenil, or any Ventolin at the moment?" Patient: "Not with me right now, no, I ran out."
Patient: "and then I have like, a hayfever, you know, and some allergies just to dust" and later: "No, no, not allergic to anything... nothing, no drugs."
Patient: "my mum has eczema."
Patient: "and my dad has asthma."

Doctor summarizes: "you've had this cold, so you've got wheezy with a cough" and they discuss missed inhalers for a week; patient has known asthma—together supporting an acute asthma exacerbation likely triggered by recent viral URI and medication lapse.

Transcript details: wheeze ("I'm feeling a bit wheezy"), chest tightness ("my chest has been feeling really tight"), mild exertional dyspnea (more SOB on stairs), and "I'm definitely not short of breath at rest."
Patient mentions hay fever and dust allergy and a recent cold, but no formal diagnosis of allergic rhinitis related to dust nor linking it to the recent URI is stated.

Patient: "I forgot to bring it with me, so I haven't really in the past week" and "they ran out"; Doctor: "you haven't got any Clenil, or any Ventolin at the moment?" confirming a one-week lapse due to being out of inhalers.
Doctor: "give you a, dose of steroids. So this is, these are tablets which, um, you can take for five days. Uh, two tablets in the morning."
Doctor: "I would quite like to... get you some, uh, Ventolin" and later: "use the Clenil Modulite in the morning, with Ventolin as a PRN ... when you need to."
Doctor: "get you some, uh, Ventolin, Clenil Modulite" and later: "once you get better from this asthma attack, you can, you can, use the Clenil Modulite in the morning."
Doctor: "the other thing I'd like to send you is a spacer" and provides verbal use instructions.
Doctor: "use the Clenil Modulite in the morning, with Ventolin as a PRN" and "If you should start to use the Ventolin more than, uh, every three hours... it's a good idea to seek medical attention."

Doctor: "Any deterioration in your symptoms, like worsening shortness of breath. Um, or just generally concerning symptoms, uh, pain in your chest tightness, uh, feeling light-headed. Uh, then, seek further medical attention anytime please."

Doctor: "I might give you some time off work as well... I think I would advise you just to, rest a little bit until you're feeling a bit better." and refers to self-certifying for the first seven days.
There is no discussion in the transcript of reinforcing allergen (dust) avoidance in the plan.
Doctor: "We can get that to you, within the hour, I would hope" referring to the prescriptions.
The transcript does not mention arranging or considering a follow-up GP or asthma review after the acute episode.
